articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
articles.summary: On the same day that Anthropic entered the public market, a painstakingly human video game became one of most successful entertainment launches of all time.
articles.full_text:
It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype.

Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.

GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ( $2.9 billion ) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ( $2 billion ).

The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.

Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda , who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.” Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids. “We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,” Ben Feder , managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch.

That’s because GTA VI was created entirely without generative AI . “We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder said. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.” As millions of people immersed themselves in Vice City, the tech industry witnessed another long-awaited moment: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public.

At Nasdaq HQ, Anthropic executives gathered to celebrate the Claude maker’s $81.3 billion IPO.

At virtually the same moment that Anthropic broke the record for the largest IPO ever, GTA VI was also breaking records with the highest-rated and best-selling game launch of all time.

But when the Anthropic team rang the bell on Thursday, the sound also signaled the end of an era in video game development, and perhaps even in the arts at large.

The AI industry operates with efficiency as its north star.

The promise of this technology is that we will be able to automate so much work that we can expand the capabilities of humanity, avoiding needless time spent tinkering with ultimately fruitless ideas.

Instead, a prompt goes into an LLM, and a response is spat out.

This technological revolution exploded into the world with some soul-crushing side effects: children are inundated with mind-numbing slop on YouTube, lawyers cite nonexistent cases in court, and tech companies like Meta lay off tens of thousands of people as part of a corporate-branded “ Year of Efficiency. ” But against the backdrop of the AI industry’s first major IPO, Rockstar has unveiled a game that about 5,000 people labored over for more than a decade.

The final product is breathtaking, looking so lifelike that it can be hard to distinguish gameplay footage from real life.

These sprawling open-world games are usually made possible by procedurally generating new landscapes and objects, but Rockstar has taken the time to painstakingly craft every detail of the world, even developing 30,000 different nonplayable characters with unique appearances and personalities.

The video game industry is already grappling with the threat of AI.

Google’s Project Genie , which launched earlier this year, allows users to create and wander around 3D worlds generated from prompts to an LLM.

The stock prices of several video game companies faltered around the time of Project Genie’s release, perhaps because of investors’ uncertainty about the future relevance of video game developers. “The notion that somehow new tools would allow an individual to push a button and generate a hit, market a hit, and bring it to many millions of consumers around the world, it’s a laughable notion,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said at the time. “It’s just never been the case with entertainment.” Zelnick’s fellow tech CEOs see different future, though.

On a Meta earnings call this year, CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised that, “soon, you’ll have an AI that understands you and [can] even generate great personalized content for you.” Elon Musk even went as far as proposing that a game like GTA VI could be made with AI. “You won’t even have to ask,” Musk wrote on X . “AI will figure what video game you’d like best.” This is the paradox of “ Grandthropic ” week.

GTA VI is so impressively vast and captivating because its developers could make mistakes, experiment, and rework ideas, even if that meant delaying the game (twice).

GTA VI was incubated with the exact inefficiencies that investors hope AI companies like Anthropic can help eradicate. “Plenty of fantastic art — video games and elsewhere — almost by definition has to be created slowly, and there’s something to having that kind of inefficiency around it,” Feder said. “Creative output requires deletion, right?

Getting to kind of a masterpiece oftentimes requires an enormous amount of deletion.

And when you’re talking about a game of the kind of complexity we’re talking about, that kind of deletion ends up being very expensive, and it is by definition not efficient.” GTA VI reeks of its own humanity – every small detail is loaded with intention, but it’s this impressive precision that keeps the world abuzz, triggering the kind of monocultural moment that has become increasingly rare in a media landscape that revolves around highly personalized social media algorithms.

The game forces the player to slow down, which is either frustrating or genius, depending on your sense of humor.

People waited more than three presidential terms for the next installment in a high-octane action franchise, only to download a 212 GB behemoth of a game in which your earliest missions involve driving around doing errands and putting up drywall to make your girlfriend happy.

Don’t worry — there are still car chases and shootouts — but in a moment when AI feels suffocating, GTA VI is such an artistic achievement that it is reaching audiences that don’t even like violent video games.

The ultimate fantasy of GTA VI is no longer to role-play as a criminal — the fantasy is just taking your time to relish the mundane and explore an expansive world that developers were given the time and space to perfect.

articles.title: Quoting Jack Despain Zhou
articles.summary: Among the many already existing effects of AI has been a great de-individualization. I open a YouTube video, and I hear Claude. I sit in a conference presentation, and I hear Claude. I open my email inbox, and I find pitches and articles from ostensibly serious people with ostensibly serious credentials attached to ostensibly serious institutions who want to publish things attached to their reputations and mine, and I see Claude .
articles.full_text:
26th November 2026 Among the many already existing effects of AI has been a great de-individualization.

I open a YouTube video, and I hear Claude.

I sit in a conference presentation, and I hear Claude.

I open my email inbox, and I find pitches and articles from ostensibly serious people with ostensibly serious credentials attached to ostensibly serious institutions who want to publish things attached to their reputations and mine, and I see Claude . — Jack Despain Zhou , Spitting in the Face of Glaude

articles.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
articles.summary: My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News. I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that.
articles.full_text:
26th November 2026 Comment My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough).

At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that.

He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted.

The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen.

You can see how dirty my screen is, too!

Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously. (Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.)

articles.full_text:
OpenAI have just released a fascinating graph showing the perplexity over time of all their released models: Here are a bunch of thoughts I have about this: Why OpenAI?

This is the most visibility we’ve ever had into the internal training metrics at a frontier lab Releasing training metrics in the name of safety is a very Anthropic move, and it’s surprising OpenAI was the one to do it first Perplexity must be measured against some specific dataset (e.g. all models will score basically zero perplexity 1 on the string “AAAAAAA….”) We therefore shouldn’t expect to be able to compare any similar data Anthropic releases with this data, except in terms of the angle on the graph 2 Is perplexity a useful measure?

Perplexity is an unsatisfying metric because it only predicts how well the model matches some held-out text: i.e. it only applies to pre-training For frontier models, the rumor is that pre-training is 50% or less of the total time and compute spent training a model; the rest is RL, which this perplexity data tells us nothing about the success of If you believe (as many do) that pre-training creates capabilities and RL merely elicits them, then perplexity would actually be a useful metric for capabilities (and indeed it does seem to go down over time as models get better) However, even if post-training does not add new capabilities, there are clearly other measures of capability that do not necessarily correlate with perplexity, like the ability to improve with chain-of-thought What is surprising about the chart?

Very few models share the same base (i.e. have the exact same perplexity).

It was a common rumor that OpenAI was post-training 4o and 4.1 into many of their models, but it looks like it was just o1 and o3 It’s interesting that 4.1 and o3 share the same base, given how great a model o3 was and how underwhelming 4.1 was You can see the point where OpenAI briefly give up on making large pretrained models at GPT-4.5, which had similar perplexity to GPT-5.3-Codex but was far less useful It’s unclear whether OpenAI chose not to pretrain further or hit some kind of internal scaling wall, but it’s interesting to consider the world where they could keep smoothly scaling on top of GPT-4.5: You can see a real acceleration in perplexity loss from GPT-5.2 on This contradicts the common wisdom 3 that OpenAI (and other labs) have largely given up on pretraining and are all-in on RL.

Clearly the pretrained base models are improving rapidly as well What does this mean for alignment?

AI safety researchers have been asking for more transparency into metrics like this for years However, I don’t really know how much it helps.

If the idea is to watch for a sudden scary drop in perplexity, only OpenAI will be in a position to notice, unless they start releasing data about the perplexity of their unreleased pretrained models (the graph shows one, but they should continue to do this) If the idea is for labs to agree on perplexity thresholds they won’t cross (as the post suggests), it will be important to get more detail on what precisely the held-out dataset is Do the improvements in the graph match how strong the models feel?

You can see a huge jump from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 (which is how it felt), then broad stagnation 4 until GPT-5.5, then rapid acceleration I personally did not feel a big jump with GPT-5.5: o3 and GPT-5.3-Codex were the “big jump” models for me However, that could be because those models were better RL-ed into using chain-of-thought tokens well, or avoiding the sycophancy trap, neither of which would show up in perplexity metrics.

I wrote this post up as dot points because I felt like I had a lot of loosely connected ideas about this news.

If you found this much harder or much easier to read than my other posts, please email me 5 about it and I will write either less or more posts in this format.

Zero log-perplexity, technically, which is the measurement in OpenAI’s graph.

Perplexity approaches 1. ↩ It would be very interesting if Anthropic’s data doesn’t show the same broad pattern of pretrains getting smarter, but I bet it does. ↩ To the point where some people are doubting the validity of the data. ↩ Except for GPT-4.5, which many people loved but did not feel particularly strong to me. ↩ You can reach me on Gmail at sean.goedecke. ↩ If you liked this post, consider subscribing to email updates about my new posts, or sharing it on Hacker News .

Here's a preview of a related post that shares tags with this one.

Reliably aligning LLMs is impossible in principle Powerful AI is unpredictable.

Your robotic butler may suddenly decide to kill you for no comprehensible reason, in the same way that Bing’s helpful chat AI would sometimes try to blackmail or seduce its users. “Solving alignment” means understanding even superintelligent AI minds well enough to be confident they’ll never do that.

As I see it, solving alignment for LLMs isn’t just impossible, it’s incoherent: we can’t even articulate what it would look like to succeed.
